title: Tate: a normal Noetherian domain complete along x with R/xR an N-2 domain is N-2
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $x\in R$. Assume (1) $R$ is a Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] normal domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]; (2) the quotient ring $R/xR$ is an integral domain and is N-2 [def-weil-pbc-japanese-domain]; (3) $R$ is $xR$-adically complete [def-weil-pbc-adically-complete-ring], i.e. the canonical map $R\to\varprojlim_nR/x^nR$ is bijective. Then $R$ is N-2: for every finite field extension $L$ [def-pc-field-extension] of the fraction field $K$ of $R$, the integral closure of $R$ in $L$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure] is a finitely generated $R$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module].

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 032P (lemma-tate-japanese, lines 45534-45589; which cites EGA 0_IV, Theorem 23.1.3), statement and proof

proof.text:
*Set-up; the case $x=0$.* If $x=0$ then $xR=0$ and $R	o R/xR$ is a ring isomorphism; it identifies the fraction fields and, for every finite extension $L$ of the fraction field, the integral closures in $L$ and their module structures, so $R$ is N-2 [def-weil-pbc-japanese-domain] because $R/xR$ is by (2). Assume from now on $x
eq0$. Since $R/xR$ is an integral domain it is not the zero ring, so $xR
eq R$ and $\mathfrak p:=xR$ is a prime ideal, nonzero as $x
eq0$ and $R$ is a domain. Let $K$ be the fraction field of $R$; its characteristic is $0$ or a prime $p$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 032P (lemma-tate-japanese, lines 45534-45589), proof: 'We may assume x ≠ 0 since otherwise the lemma is trivial'

proof.text: *Characteristic $0$.* Suppose $\operatorname{char}K=0$ and let $L/K$ be a finite extension. By [lem-weil-pbc-char-zero-field-extension-separable] $L$ is separable over $K$ in the sense of [def-weil-pbc-separable-field-extension]; applied to the finitely generated subextension $K'=L$, whose transcendence basis over $K$ [def-weil-pbc-transcendence-basis] is empty because $L/K$ is algebraic (every element of a finite-dimensional extension satisfies a nonzero polynomial), this says $L/K$ is separable algebraic [def-weil-pbc-separable-algebraic-extension]. As $R$ is a Noetherian normal domain by (1), [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-normal-separable-integral-closure-finite] shows that the integral closure of $R$ in $L$ is a finitely generated $R$-module. Hence $R$ is N-2 [def-weil-pbc-japanese-domain]. (This is the source's appeal to Lemma 032M, whose proof is Lemma 032L plus separability in characteristic zero; a normal domain is trivially N-1.)

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 032P (lemma-tate-japanese, lines 45534-45589), proof: 'If the characteristic of K is zero the lemma follows from (1), see Lemma lemma-domain-char-zero-N-1-2' (Tag 032M, proved from Lemma 032L)

proof.text: *Characteristic $p>0$: reduction to purely inseparable extensions.* Suppose $\operatorname{char}K=p>0$. By [lem-weil-pbc-n2-char-p-purely-inseparable-criterion], applied to the Noetherian domain $R$, it suffices to show: for every finite purely inseparable extension $L/K$ [def-weil-pbc-finite-purely-inseparable-extension] the integral closure of $R$ in $L$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure] is a finitely generated $R$-module. Steps 4–12 prove this for a fixed such $L$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 032P (lemma-tate-japanese, lines 45534-45589), proof: 'Hence we may assume that the characteristic of K is p > 0, and we may apply Lemma lemma-domain-char-p-N-1-2' (Tag 032N)

proof.text: *An exponent $q$ and the enlargement of $L$ (the details of 'by enlarging $L$ if necessary').* Let $b_1,\dots,b_m$ be a $K$-basis of $L$; by [def-weil-pbc-finite-purely-inseparable-extension] there are $e_i\ge0$ with $b_i^{p^{e_i}}\in K$. Put $e=\max_ie_i$ and $q=p^e$; then $b_i^q=(b_i^{p^{e_i}})^{p^{e-e_i}}\in K$, and since $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^q$ is the iterated Frobenius, a ring endomorphism of $L$ [def-weil-ring-frobenius], every $\alpha=\sum c_ib_i$ ($c_i\in K$) has $\alpha^q=\sum c_i^qb_i^q\in K$: $L^q\subseteq K$. Choose an algebraic closure $\Omega$ of $L$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure] and $y\in\Omega$ with $y^q=x$ (a root of the nonconstant polynomial $T^q-x$). Let $L'=L(y)\subseteq\Omega$ be the subfield generated by $L$ and $y$; $y$ is algebraic over $L$, so $L'/L$ is finite [lem-weil-pbc-algebraic-generators-finite-extension], and $L'/K$ is finite by [lem-weil-pbc-field-degree-multiplicativity]. The ring $L[y]$ is a finite-dimensional $L$-algebra contained in a field, hence a domain in which multiplication by a nonzero element is an injective, so surjective, $L$-linear endomorphism; so $L[y]$ is a field and $L'=L[y]$. Thus every element of $L'$ is $\sum_ia_iy^i$ with $a_i\in L$, and its $q$-th power is $\sum_ia_i^qx^i\in K$. Hence $L'/K$ is finite purely inseparable with $L'^q\subseteq K$, and $L'$ contains $y$ with $y^q=x$. If $S'$ is the integral closure of $R$ in $L'$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure], the integral closure of $R$ in $L$ is $S'\cap L$, an $R$-submodule of $S'$; so if $S'$ is a finitely generated $R$-module, so is $S'\cap L$, by [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-submodule-finite] ($R$ Noetherian). Replacing $L$ by $L'$ we may and do assume: $L^q\subseteq K$ and there is $y\in L$ with $y^q=x$. Let $S$ be the integral closure of $R$ in $L$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 032P (lemma-tate-japanese, lines 45534-45589), proof: 'Let q be a power of p such that L^q ⊂ K. By enlarging L if necessary we may assume there exists an element y ∈ L such that y^q = x'

proof.text: *Basic properties of $S$.* $S$ is a subring of $L$ containing $R$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure], hence a domain, and by [lem-weil-pbc-integral-closure-finite-extension-normal] $L$ is a fraction field of $S$. (a) For $f\in S$ we have $f^q\in R$: $f^q\in L^q\subseteq K$ is integral over $R$ (a power of an integral element; $S$ is a ring), and $R$ is integrally closed in $K$ by (1) [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. (b) $y\in S$, being a root of the monic $T^q-x\in R[T]$, and $y\neq0$ since $y^q=x\neq0$. (c) $xS\cap R=xR$: if $r=xs$ with $r\in R$, $s\in S$, then $s=r/x\in K$ is integral over $R$, so $s\in R$ by normality.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 032P (lemma-tate-japanese, lines 45534-45589), proof: implicit in 'It is clear that q = {f ∈ S | f^q ∈ p} = yS since y^q = x' and in 'an element in the intersection has qth power contained in ∩x^nR'

proof.text: *The prime $\mathfrak q=yS$ over $\mathfrak p$ (the source's 'it is clear').* Put $\mathfrak q=yS$. Claim: for $f\in S$, $f\in\mathfrak q\iff f^q\in\mathfrak p$. If $f=ys$ ($s\in S$) then $f^q=xs^q\in xR$ since $s^q\in R$ by Step 5(a). Conversely if $f^q=xr$ with $r\in R$, then $g=f/y\in L$ satisfies $g^q=f^q/x=r\in R$, so $g$ is a root of the monic $T^q-r$ and $g\in S$, i.e. $f=yg\in yS$. Consequences: $1\notin\mathfrak q$ since $1\notin\mathfrak p$; if $fg\in\mathfrak q$ then $f^qg^q=(fg)^q\in\mathfrak p$ with $f^q,g^q\in R$, so as $\mathfrak p$ is prime $f^q\in\mathfrak p$ or $g^q\in\mathfrak p$, i.e. $f\in\mathfrak q$ or $g\in\mathfrak q$. So $\mathfrak q$ is a prime ideal of $S$. For $r\in R$: $r\in\mathfrak q\iff r^q\in\mathfrak p\iff r\in\mathfrak p$ ($\mathfrak p$ prime), so $\mathfrak q\cap R=\mathfrak p$. (The source deduces from Lemma 0BRA that $\mathfrak q$ is the unique prime over $\mathfrak p$; uniqueness is not used below, only that $yS$ is a prime lying over $\mathfrak p$, which is verified here directly.)

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 032P (lemma-tate-japanese, lines 45534-45589), proof: 'there is a unique prime ideal q ⊂ S lying over the prime ideal p = xR. It is clear that q = {f ∈ S | f^q ∈ p} = yS since y^q = x'

proof.text: *$R_{\mathfrak p}$ is a one-dimensional Noetherian local domain.* $R_{\mathfrak p}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] is a local ring, a domain (a subring of $K$), and Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-noetherian]. Height of $\mathfrak p$: by [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-height-quotient-bound] with $t=1$, $f_1=x$, $J=xR=\mathfrak p$ and $\mathfrak P=\mathfrak p$, $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)\le\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p/J)+1=\operatorname{ht}((0)\subset R/xR)+1=1$, the zero ideal having height $0$ (a chain of primes contained in $(0)$ has only the term $(0)$). And $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)\ge1$ by the chain $(0)\subsetneq\mathfrak p$ ($R$ is a domain, $\mathfrak p\ne0$). By [lem-weil-pbc-localization-dimension-chains-below-prime] the Krull dimension [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring] of $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)=1$. (The source states here that $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is a discrete valuation ring (00PD), and then that $S_{\mathfrak q}$ is Noetherian (Krull–Akizuki 00PG) and a discrete valuation ring; the rest of the proof uses only that $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is a one-dimensional Noetherian local domain, which is what Lemma 031F asks for, so these further assertions are not needed and not stated.)

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 032P (lemma-tate-japanese, lines 45534-45589), proof: 'Observe that R_p is a discrete valuation ring by Lemma lemma-characterize-dvr. Then S_q is Noetherian by Krull-Akizuki ... a discrete valuation ring'

proof.text: *$\kappa(\mathfrak q)/\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ is finite.* Since $\mathfrak q\cap R=\mathfrak p$ (Step 6), $R\setminus\mathfrak p\subseteq S\setminus\mathfrak q$, so the inclusion $R\subseteq S$ extends to an injective homomorphism of domains $\varphi:R_{\mathfrak p}\to S_{\mathfrak q}$, both rings being subrings of $L$ ($R_{\mathfrak p}\subseteq K$). The fraction field of $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is $K$, and that of $S_{\mathfrak q}$ is $L$, as $S\subseteq S_{\mathfrak q}\subseteq L$ and $L$ is a fraction field of $S$ [lem-weil-pbc-integral-closure-finite-extension-normal]; $\dim_KL<\infty$. The maximal ideal $\mathfrak n=\mathfrak qS_{\mathfrak q}$ satisfies $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak n)=\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}$: if $r/s\in\mathfrak qS_{\mathfrak q}$ with $r\in R$, $s\in R\setminus\mathfrak p$, write $r/s=f/t$ with $f\in\mathfrak q$, $t\in S\setminus\mathfrak q$; then $rt=sf\in\mathfrak q$ and $t\notin\mathfrak q$ give $r\in\mathfrak q\cap R=\mathfrak p$; the other inclusion is clear. By Step 7, [lem-weil-pbc-dim-one-residue-field-extensions-finite] (3) applies to $\varphi$ and $\mathfrak n$: $\kappa(\mathfrak q)=S_{\mathfrak q}/\mathfrak qS_{\mathfrak q}$ is a finite-dimensional field extension of $\kappa(\mathfrak p)=R_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime].

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 032P (lemma-tate-japanese, lines 45534-45589), proof: 'By Lemma lemma-finite-extension-residue-fields-dimension-1 we see that κ(q)/κ(p) is a finite field extension' (Tag 031F)

proof.text: *$S/yS$ is a finitely generated $R$-module.* By [lem-weil-pbc-prime-residue-field-algebra] (b), $R/\mathfrak p\to\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ is injective and makes $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ a fraction field of the domain $R/\mathfrak p=R/xR$, and $S/\mathfrak q\to\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ is injective; these maps are compatible with $R/\mathfrak p\to S/\mathfrak q$ and $\kappa(\mathfrak p)\to\kappa(\mathfrak q)$. By Step 8 and hypothesis (2) ($R/xR$ is N-2 [def-weil-pbc-japanese-domain]), the integral closure $S'$ of $R/xR$ in $\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure] is a finitely generated $R/xR$-module, hence a finitely generated $R$-module [lem-weil-pbc-finite-module-over-finite-algebra] ($R/xR$ is generated by $1$ as an $R$-module). Every element of $S/\mathfrak q$ is integral over $R/\mathfrak p$ (reduce modulo $\mathfrak q$ a monic equation over $R$ of a lift in $S$), so its image lies in $S'$: $S/yS=S/\mathfrak q$ is isomorphic to an $R$-submodule of $S'$, hence finitely generated over $R$ by [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-submodule-finite].

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 032P (lemma-tate-japanese, lines 45534-45589), proof: 'Hence the integral closure S' ⊂ κ(q) of R/xR is finite over R/xR by assumption (2). Since S/yS ⊂ S' this implies that S/yS is finite over R'

proof.text: *$S/xS$ is a finitely generated $R/xR$-module.* By induction on $n\ge1$, $S/y^nS$ is a finitely generated $R$-module; $n=1$ is Step 9. For the induction step consider $S/yS\xrightarrow{\mu}S/y^{n+1}S\xrightarrow{\pi}S/y^nS\to0$, with $\mu(s+yS)=y^ns+y^{n+1}S$ (well defined) and $\pi$ the projection. $\pi$ is surjective, $\pi\circ\mu=0$, and $\ker\pi=y^nS/y^{n+1}S=\operatorname{im}\mu$. (Also $\mu$ is injective: $y^ns=y^{n+1}t$ gives $s=yt$ as $S$ is a domain and $y\ne0$, so $y^iS/y^{i+1}S\cong S/yS$ as in the source.) By [lem-weil-pbc-module-finite-extension-of-finite] $S/y^{n+1}S$ is finitely generated over $R$. For $n=q$: $y^q=x$, so $S/xS$ is a finitely generated $R$-module; as $x$ annihilates it, the same generators generate it over $R/xR$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 032P (lemma-tate-japanese, lines 45534-45589), proof: 'Note that S/y^nS has a finite filtration whose subquotients are the modules y^iS/y^{i+1}S ≅ S/yS. Hence we see that each S/y^nS is finite over R. In particular S/xS is finite over R'

proof.text: *$\bigcap_{n\ge1}x^nS=0$.* Hypothesis (3) [def-weil-pbc-adically-complete-ring] says that $R\to\varprojlim_nR/x^nR$ is bijective; its kernel is $\bigcap_nx^nR$, so $\bigcap_nx^nR=0$. Let $f\in\bigcap_nx^nS$; for each $n$ write $f=x^ns_n$ with $s_n\in S$; then $f^q=x^{nq}s_n^q\in x^nR$ since $s_n^q\in R$ (Step 5(a)). So $f^q\in\bigcap_nx^nR=0$, and $f=0$ as $L$ is a field. (The source cites Krull's intersection theorem 00IP here, which is stated for Noetherian local rings while $R$ need not be local; the vanishing of $\bigcap_nx^nR$ is part of hypothesis (3), so no intersection theorem is needed.)

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 032P (lemma-tate-japanese, lines 45534-45589), proof: 'Also, it is clear that ∩x^nS = (0) since an element in the intersection has qth power contained in ∩x^nR = (0) (Lemma lemma-intersect-powers-ideal-module-zero)'

proof.text: *Conclusion.* Apply [lem-weil-pbc-finite-over-complete-ring] to $A=R$, $I=xR$ and the $R$-module $M=S$: (1) $R$ is $xR$-adically complete by hypothesis (3) [def-weil-pbc-adically-complete-ring]; (2) $\bigcap_n(xR)^nS=\bigcap_nx^nS=0$ by Step 11; (3) $S/(xR)S=S/xS$ is a finitely generated $R/xR$-module by Step 10. Hence $S$ is a finitely generated $R$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. By Step 4 the integral closure of $R$ in the original finite purely inseparable $L$ is finitely generated, and by Step 3 $R$ is N-2 [def-weil-pbc-japanese-domain].

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 032P (lemma-tate-japanese, lines 45534-45589), proof: 'Thus we may apply Lemma lemma-finite-over-complete-ring to conclude that S is finite over R, and we win' (Tag 031D)
